titleStmt.title: Scaling, Packetizers and Aggregation in Network Calculus

analytic.title: Scaling, Packetizers and Aggregation in Network Calculus

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Real-time systems often consist of numerous subsystems engaged in extensive data exchange. Despite their complexity, a critical challenge lies in effectively incorporating realtime constraints within these systems. To address this challenge, designers typically conduct analyses to establish upper bounds on delays, ensuring they remain within the deadlines of incoming requests. However, adopting a pessimistic approach often results in over-dimensioning the systems. Then, to reduce the pessimism, we want to take into account the fact that a subsystem cannot propagate more requests/data than it can execute. This phenomenon is well-known in network analysis as it reduces the burst of data. As a consequence, this notion is easier to grasp in theories developed to compute delay bounds in networks. That is why we choose, in this paper, to perform the analysis using the Network Calculus theory, since it offers the possibility to easily aggregate flows (i.e. sum flows) and then take into account the phenomenon of smoothing the traffic. To handle tasks and networks, our model relies on packetization and workload scaling. In this paper, we improve some results regarding the already existing elements of Network Calculus and the aggregation. Also, we update and complete definitions and results related to workload scaling.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Nowadays, real-time systems are increasingly complex and can be composed of a large number of subsystems exchanging a large number of requests/data. One of the challenges is to be able to guarantee that each request will meet its deadline. To do so, several analyses of such real-time systems can allow designers to compute worst-case delay upper bounds and make sure the time constraints are met (if the bounds are lower than the deadlines). However, the analysis can be pessimistic and can lead to oversizing of the system if the bounds are too large wrt. the worst case.

To reduce this pessimism, a little-considered phenomenon could be taken into account: a subsystem cannot propagate more requests/data than it can execute. It means that two propagated requests from the same element of the system are, at least, separated by the time to execute the first one. In a network, it is a phenomenon known as it reduces the bursts of data, i.e. the accumulation of data at the same time.

In this paper, we model this phenomenon in distributed systems where tasks communicate through a network and some tasks are released by the reception of a message or the end of the execution of a previous one (released task chains). As a consequence, we will be looking at task chains communicating through a network and computing delay bounds on these chains.

Various theories have been used to analyse such chains. Above all, we choose to analyse chains using the Network Calculus theory. It is mainly motivated by the fact that, in the future, we want to perform bounds on chains communicating through networks like Time Sensitive Networking networks (TSN, [1]). One of the strengths of Network Calculus is the possibility to aggregate requests modelled as flows (i.e. to sum flows) easily and use the build-in shaping to model the fact that the total output of a system is limited by its maximal capacity and, therefore, it is easy to consider the phenomenon described above.

To model release task chains in Network Calculus, we first need to model tasks. Inspired by [2], we introduced the arrival and departure functions for these tasks based on job characteristics (release time, completion time, and workload). To suggest a model of task chains, we use existing network elements (putting in sequence a server, a packetizer and a multiplier). A packetizer is a network element that waits for the end of the execution of the request before releasing it instantaneously. A multiplier (called scaling function in [3]) is an element of the system that can change the size of a flow.
To be able to benefit from the smoothing/shaping capacity in this context, we extend properties of this packetizer and multiplier regarding aggregated flows.

The main contributions of this paper are 1) another model of tasks and tasks chain using Network Calculus, 2) new packetizer's results regarding the aggregation (sum) of flows, 3) an update of scaling (renamed multiplier) to model task chains in Network Calculus. The paper is organised as follows. Section II presents our model of the release task chain with Network Calculus. A state of the art is presented in Section III and notations are introduced in Section IV. Next, Section V reminds the Network Calculus basics with new results regarding the aggregation in the packetizer. Then, Section VI presents an element modifying the workload, the multiplier, inspired by the scaling function from [3]. Finally, we use the proven results in Section VII with a sample. II. SYSTEM MODEL a) Model of tasks and release task chains: A task, which we will note T , is an infinite sequence of jobs: (J n ) n∈N . And a job, J , is characterised by a tuple ⟨r; w; e⟩ where r is the release time (i.e. the time when the job is ready to start), w the workload (i.e. the number of CPU cycles required to execute the job) and e ≥ r the completion time (i.e. the time when the all workload has been served). We assume that the jobs of a task are ordered in ascending order of the release times.

Regarding the task chains, there are two types, both predicated on a precedence relation between tasks (T → T ′ ): "release task chain" where the end of the execution of a job from T releases a job of T ′ and "triggered task chain" where the jobs are independently released but each job of T ′ uses the results of the last executed jobs of T . Here, the release time chains are considered, i.e. two tasks T , T ′ are chained if the completion time of the job J i of the task T is the release time of the job J ′ i of the task T ′ : ∀n ∈ N, r ′ n = e n . b) Model in Network Calculus: Inspired by [2], we suggest a way to model the tasks using Network Calculus. When modelling a network, a cumulative curve represents the cumulative amount of data up to the current instant. When modelling a task T , it represents the amount of workload (number of CPU cycles) generated by a task. Then, it can be defined as
div.formula: A T (t) = n∈N|rn≤t w n .
div.p: Network Calculus models the task scheduling by counting the work done into the cumulative curve D T (cf. Figure 1). To model a task chain T → T ′ , we need to derive the arrival A T ′ from A T . First, we can derive the completion times of jobs from A T using the Network Calculus element called packetizer (designed to store bits up to having a full packet, which is equivalent as storing work up to full execution). And to generate the workload w ′ i of the next job, one just have to multiply the executed workload w i by w ′ i /w i . Figure 1 illustrates this sequence of elements that model the task chain.

div.head: III. RELATED WORK
div.p: This section is organised following the models on which the analyses are based. It starts with the curve-based models, continues with other models and ends with cooperation models.

Curve-based models Real-time Calculus (RTC) has been developed as a fork of Network Calculus devoted to the analysis of complex real-time systems. An equivalence between the main equations can be found in [4], [5]. To deal with the task chain, and especially the change of workload, it uses dedicated workload curves per task (γ, γ ′ for tasks τ , τ ′ ), and the composition γ ′ •γ -1 corresponds to our sequence of packetizer and multiplier elements [6], [7]. They do not consider the aggregation of flows. In Network Calculus, these elements have been studied per se and come with several interesting properties (cf. Sections V-D and VI-A). In the Compositional Performance Analysis (CPA), the model is based on the notion of Event Stream, often denoted η, each event being either a task release or a message reception. Modelling the fact that one task T releases task T ′ is done by transforming the event stream of T , often denoted η, into another event stream η ′ , being the event stream of T ′ . This model is well-established, and most work is done on the response time analysis of such chains, as in [8] (focusing on chains where all tasks do not have the same priorities) and [9] (considering also blocking due to sub-calls). Conversely to Network Calculus, the workload associated with each job is not in the event stream itself, but as a separate parameter, often denoted q, and added when doing the response time analysis. It then does not have to face the problem of the difference in workload size between releasing and released jobs. But when considering an aggregation of several tasks of different sizes, the analysis must consider each individual workload.

Other models to analyse release task chains In [10], the authors consider only periodic tasks using three parameters: the workload, the period and a deadline. Each task can be a subsequence of tasks defined also by a workload and a deadline, and they add a priority. Then, a framework is proposed to analyse the schedulability using the notion of busy periods. However, only periodic tasks with fixed priority scheduling are considered. In our manuscript, we try to model the task and task chain with another framework and be as generic as possible regarding the scheduling policy. In [11], the aim is not simply to compute the response time of a chain, but to take into account the chain to count deadline misses in a weakly hard real-time system. Then, in [12], the task chain is formally defined in Definition 3.2 (it is quite similar to our definition except that it is more specific because, for instance, they include a deadline and the execution policy in the definition of the task chain). They also define the task model in Definition 3.1, considering that a task is defined only by a priority and a worst-case execution time where we choose to base our model on [2]. Since then, [12] suggests an analysis of the task chain based on the busy window. A holistic approach, analysing a system made of different computing resources can also be done [13].

Model cooperation It is shown in [14] how two methods (CPA and RTC) can be combined to analyse a single case study by analysing each element with one or the other method. One can also analyse each element with two methods and get the best of both [15] with CPA and Network Calculus. The task response time analysis can be used to generate a data flow arrival curve, taking into account the task scheduling [16].

Modelling task in Network Calculus A formal equivalence between the subset of Network Calculus and Classical Response Time Analysis presented in the [2]. Our work extends the results to analyse chains of tasks using only the Network Calculus elements that are already in place.

div.head: IV. NOTATIONS
div.p: We first introduce some notations useful for the following sections.

First, R and R + denote the set of reals and non-negative reals, respectively. N denotes the set of natural integers and Z the set of integers. • represents the composition operator, i.e. let f, g be two functions from R + to R + and t a non-negative real, f • g(t) = f (g(t)). δ 0 : R + → R + denotes the function such that δ 0 (0) = 0 and ∀t > 0, δ 0 (t) = +∞.
Also, we note U : N → R the function associated to a sequence
div.formula: (U n ) n∈N such that U (n) = U n . Then, we will either note U n or U (n).
div.p: Finally, F denotes the set of functions from R + to R + piecewise continuous, R the subset of F such that the functions are right continuous. And, for any X ⊆ F, X ↑ denotes the subset of X such that the functions are non-decreasing and X 0 denotes the subset of X such that ∀f ∈ X 0 , f (0) = 0.

div.head: V. NETWORK CALCULUS BASICS
div.p: Here start the Network Calculus basics based on [5] and [17]. This section gives the base of the Network Calculus that we need in the following. First, we introduce mathematical basics, then we give definitions and properties regarding the cumulative curves, the arrival curves, and the network elements (servers, packetizers and multipliers).

div.head: A. Operators
div.p: In the Network Calculus theory, the main operators are the (min,plus) convolution (noted * ), the (min,plus) deconvolution (noted ⊘), the (max,plus) convolution (noted * ) and the (max,plus) deconvolution (noted ⊘), defined respectively, for all f, g ∈ F two functions and for all t ∈ R + , by
div.formula: (f * g)(t) def = inf 0≤v≤t {f (t -v) + g(v)} , (f ⊘ g)(t) def = sup v≥0 {f (t + v) -g(v)} . (f * g)(t) def = sup 0≤v≤t {f (t -v) + g(v)} , (f ⊘ g)(t) def = inf v≥0 {f (t + v) -g(v)} .

div.p: Finally, we add a properties to bound the convolution of a sub/super additive function.

div.p: Here, continuity seems to be problematic in respecting the hypothesis of Property 1. However, in Network Calculus, it is common to consider all functions as left-continuous or right-continuous and not mix different continuities in the same model. It is enough to meet the assumptions because if we use left-continuous functions, then f and g are left-continuous, and if we consider only right-continuous ones, h is rightcontinuous.
In the rest of the paper, we assume that all the functions have the same continuity, either right or left continuous.

div.head: B. Data model: cumulative and arrival curves
div.p: In Network Calculus, flows are modelled by cumulative functions A ∈ F ↑ 0 such that A(t) counts the total amount of data of a flow passed through some observation point up to time t. One of the strengths of the Network Calculus theory is the possibility to aggregate flows, i.e. the sum of two cumulative curves remains a cumulative curve.
Let us continue with arrival curves. The notion of arrival curves is introduced to bound the cumulative curve on any interval of time and for
div.formula: A ∈ F ↑ 0 : a cumulative curve, α ∈ F ↑ , respectively α ∈ F ↑ , is a maximal, respectively minimal, arrival curve for A, if ∀t, d ∈ R + : α(d) ≤ A(t + d) -A(t) ≤ α(d).
div.p: From Proposition 5.2 in [5], a property regarding the minimum of arrival curves will be useful.

div.p: A ∈ F ↑ 0 be a cumulative curve, and α ∈ F ↑ be a maximal arrival curve for A. Then, if α ′ is another maximal arrival curve of A, α ∧ α is also a maximal arrival curve for A.

div.head: C. Servers (size-invariant)
div.p: The common servers in the Network Calculus theory are size invariant elements, i.e. the output data size is exactly the same as the input ones. With this assumption, the departure amount is at any time less or equal to the arrival amount. Network elements able to change the size of the processed data will be called "multipliers" and will be defined in Section VI.

div.p: A packetizer is also a size-invariant element that stores bits up to the end of a packet and instantaneously delivers the whole packet, considering that the flow is composed of a sequence of packets. We can, then, consider the packet length sequence as the function that associates the number of packets with its cumulative amount of data.

div.head: VI. NON-SIZE INVARIANT ELEMENTS
div.p: As mentioned in Section V-C, the servers in the Network Calculus theory are size invariant elements, i.e. the output data size are exactly the same as the input ones. This section will introduce multipliers, a renaming of scaling servers. The reasons why we adapt the results from [3] are detailed in [21, Section VI.A].

div.head: A. Multiplier definition
div.p: The notion of the multiplier is inspired by the scaling servers from [3]. However, to go further with this notion, as explained in the following, we need to adapt the notation and results.

div.head: Definition 8 (Multiplier
div.formula: ). A multiplier M is a size-variant element such that ∀(A, D) ∈ M , ∀t, t ′ ∈ R + : A(t) = A(t ′ ) =⇒ D(t) = D(t ′ ).(2)
div.p: The condition in eq. ( 2) implies that there is no data output if there is no data input during the same time interval.
Then, we can introduce the multiplier function as followed.
Definition 9 (Multiplier function). Let M be a multiplier, and (A, D) ∈ M . Then, a multiplier function for (A, D) is a non-decreasing function M A,D : R
div.formula: + → R + such that ∀t : M A,D (A(t)) = D(t).
div.p: This definition is slightly different from the one of [3]: "a scaling function S assigns an amount of scaled data S(a) to an amount of data a.". The first reason is related to nondeterminism: a scaling element may have different outputs depending on the input. For example, the CAN MAC layer introduces one bit of opposite value after a sequence of five equal bits. If C denotes such a layer, then, for a given input A (representing some amount of bits arrivals at each instant), several departure D, D ′ may exist, depending on the values of the bit sequence, not only on the amount. The second reason is related to maths: giving A and D is not sufficient to define a function: if A is not continuous, it will exist some a ∈ R + such that there is not t with A(t) = a, and then, S(a) is not defined. Finally, we chose to rename the "scaling" as "multiplier" to avoid any confusion with the server (we used to abbreviate the network element with the first letter) and because we slightly changed the definition of the network element.
Then, we can define the multiplier curves.
Definition 10 (Multiplier curves). Let M be a multiplier. Then, a function µ ∈ F ↑ (resp. µ ∈ F ↑ ) is a maximal (resp. minimal)
div.formula: multiplier curve if ∀t, d ∈ R + , ∀(A, D) ∈ M : µ(A(t + d) - A(t)) ≤ D(t + d) -D(t) ≤ µ(A(t + d) -A(t)).

div.head: VII. USE OF RESULTS
div.p: This section aims to compare the results of the previous model in Network Calculus with the results of the CPA theory. To do that, we will analyse a system illustrated in Figure 4 composed of:

• CPU1: a Static Priority Preemptive CPU with three periodic tasks (T 1, T 2, T 3) in ascending order of priority. • CPU2: a Static Priority Preemptive CPU with three periodic tasks (T 4, T 5) in ascending order of priority. • CAN Bus: a Static Priority Non Preemptive bus with three release tasks (T ′ 2, T ′ 3, T ′ 4) respectively released by (T 2, T 3, T 4) in ascending order of priority. • CPU3: a Static Priority Preemptive CPU with three released tasks (T ′′ 2, T ′′ 3, T ′′ 4) respectively released by (T ′ 2, T ′ 3, T ′ 4) in ascending order of priority. The strength of the Network Calculus is to be able to aggregate flows. Here, this example is interesting thanks to the possibility of aggregating T 2 and T 3 to compute an upper bound on the delay of T 4.
We will use a set of parameters detailed in Table I.

The aim is to calculate the worst-case execution times of the three task chains: C2: T 2 → T 2 ′ → T 2 ′′ , C3: T 3 → T 3 ′ → T 3 ′′ , and C4: T 4 → T 4 ′ → T 4 ′′ . This system will be analysed with 1) the CPA method (the results will be noted CPA), with 2) current Network Calculus methods, i.e. considering SFA and TFA combined with [3] and keeping the minimum) (the results will be noted NC) and 3) with the same Network Calculus algorithms plus our results. Note that as the tasks T 2 and T 3 come from the same source and have the same route, the Network Calculus allows us to compute the worst-case execution time considering the aggregate flow composed of these two tasks. The results of the three analyses are given in Table II. The code is given in [21], Appendix B. In this case, the TFA algorithm always gives the smaller bounds, but no generic conclusion can be derived from this simple case (cf. [22]), First, we note that the worst-case execution time of the task chains C1 and C2 are the same regardless of the analysis used. However, we see a difference with the task chain C4.

As we said, one of the pluses of the Network Calculus theory is the easy handling of aggregate flows. Shaping tasks T 2 and T 3 and the released one allows the Network Calculus to improve the analysis results. Note that the Network Calculus cannot improve the results without aggregation and is more pessimistic than CPA.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we present novel results concerning packetization/scaling and flow aggregation within the Network Calculus framework. These results were motivated by enhancing the bounds of released task chains, considering the inherent limitation that a subsystem cannot transmit more data than it can process. Additionally, we demonstrate the efficacy of our results through an illustrative example, showcasing the benefits of flow aggregation in Network Calculus. All the presented work will allow us to analyse tasks, task chains, and, by extension, some parts of the system using only Network Calculus, reducing the loss of information between theories when sharing the results.
